abstract: Deep learning methods for pathology are constrained by the limited availability and high cost of large-scale pixel-level annotations. Synthetic data can alleviate this limitation, but existing pipelines often lack reliable quality control and remain weakly connected to downstream analysis. To address these issues, we propose a three-stage framework that integrates automated data screening, generative representation learning, and efficient adaptation to downstream tasks. First, we develop a pathology agent system to assess image quality and filter samples, resulting in TCGA-200K, a dataset containing 217,030 pathology patches selected from the public TCGA repository. Second, we train a generative model on the screened data. In addition to image synthesis, its backbone learns structural and semantic representations that can be transferred to downstream tasks. Third, we adapt the pretrained generative backbone to semantic segmentation using a lightweight task-specific head. We further introduce PathSeg-380K, a semantic segmentation dataset with expert annotations for approximately 380,000 cells across 12 cell types. Experiments on multiple pathology datasets show that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art segmentation performance. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/script-Yang/Agent-GenPath.

sections.body: The section motivates the work. Deep learning models for pathology depend on large expert annotations, which are costly and scarce. The authors identify two gaps in existing synthetic-data pipelines: training images are not reliably quality-checked, and generative models are used only as samplers, disconnected from downstream tasks. They propose three stages: an agent-based screening mechanism that retains only high-scoring images, generative training on the curated set so that the backbone serves as an encoder, and a lightweight task-specific head for semantic segmentation. The section states these claims as design motivation. Quantitative evidence appears in later sections.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Annotation scarcity limits pathology deep learning, motivating screening, generative pretraining, and transfer to segmentation.

sections.body: The section describes three stages. **Stage I** scores patches on cell presence, stain quality and histologic clarity. An expert agent labels a small pilot set on a 1 to 5 scale, a ResNet-50 regressor trained with mean squared error scores the remaining pool, and a patch is kept only if all three scores fall in the top k% of their distributions. This yields 217,030 patches. **Stage II** trains a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) with flow matching on these patches. **Stage III** extracts features from DiT blocks 2, 5, 8 and 11, passes them through a lightweight multi-level decoder, and trains with cross-entropy plus Dice loss. The section reports no limitations. It describes the regressor only as approximating the agent.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Agent-filtered patches train a Diffusion Transformer, whose multi-level features feed a segmentation decoder.

sections.body: The section tests each component on PanNuke and PathSeg-380K. On 600 patches, the agent reaches Spearman correlations of 0.782, 0.811 and 0.829 against pathologist consensus, and the regressor reaches a weighted kappa of 0.912 against the agent. Keeping the top 10% of patches gives FID 23.96 and 55.46% mIoU on PanNuke. The top 5% gives 55.03% mIoU, which the authors attribute to reduced diversity. The full model reaches 55.45% mIoU on PathSeg-380K. Against U-Net, CellViT, CONCH and UNI, it reports the best overlap metrics on both datasets, with significance under a paired t-test. The generative prior alone adds 7.59 mIoU points on PanNuke.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Transferred generative features reach 55.46% mIoU on PanNuke, versus 47.19% when trained from scratch.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the framework. Agent-based screening builds TCGA-200K, the DiT backbone learns pathology-specific representations, and a lightweight head transfers them to segmentation. The authors cite results on PanNuke and PathSeg-380K as evidence that generative pretraining serves both image synthesis and downstream analysis. Stated future work covers classification and survival analysis, along with more efficient agent-based curation to reduce screening costs while preserving data quality across institutions and staining protocols. The conclusion adds no new experiments.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper concludes that generative pretraining serves both synthesis and segmentation, and lists classification and survival analysis as future work.
